overview.text: Mechanical stress describes the intensity of forces carried inside a material when external loads push, pull, or shear it. In a simple uniform case, stress equals force divided by the area over which it acts (σ = F/A), so its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), or newton per square metre. Strain, by contrast, measures deformation—such as the fractional change in a rod’s length—and has no units. Stress may be tensile (pulling), compressive (squeezing), or shear (sliding layers). In the elastic, approximately linear range, stress is proportional to strain; the slope is an elastic modulus, such as Young’s modulus for stretching or compression. This relationship helps engineers estimate material deformation under load, while excessive stress can cause permanent deformation or failure.

key_facts.text: For tensile or compressive stress, the force acts perpendicular to a cross-section; in the simple uniform case, stress is that force divided by the area.
Shear stress comes from forces parallel to a surface and tends to make neighboring parts of a solid slide past one another.
A rod’s tensile strain is its change in length divided by its original length, making strain a unitless measure of deformation.
Young’s modulus is the stress-to-strain ratio for tensile or compressive deformation in the linear elastic range; shear deformation has its own shear modulus.
Loads that vary or repeat, and flaws in a material, can increase the risk of stress-related damage or failure.
